newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch aghast at wave of family child killings.
newsitem.headline: Dutch aghast at wave of family child killings.

text.p: A wave of killings of children by their parents is spurring soul-searching in the Netherlands and sparking debate over media coverage of family tragedies.
Child protection agencies have noted a sharp jump in calls from parents concerned about the safety of their children.

"We have had a big increase in people calling us, many are very worried and frightened for their children," a spokeswoman for the Council for Child Protection said on Wednesday. "There are people who are really afraid of their partner."
In the latest of five cases already this year a 41-year-old father from Hoofddorp, near Amsterdam, admitted on Tuesday to killing his wife and six-year-old daughter.
The wave began on January 15, when police found the bodies of three children, boys of eight and nine and a girl of seven, dead at their family home in the same town.
Their parents, who failed in their own suicide attempts, admitted killing the children, saying they had never recovered from the death of a fourth child from leukaemia two years ago.
Four days later, police arrested a 36-year-old woman accused of suffocating her daughter of nine. They gave no indication as to her motive.

On January 24, a 43-year-old divorced father shot his two sons, seven and nine, and himself in woods near his home during a custodial visit and on February 6 another divorced man killed his eight-year-old son and five-year-old daughter.

There were just four similar killings in the Netherlands during 1996 and the sudden cluster of cases has led to anguished discussion over the social causes and the effects of the wide Dutch media coverage they have received.
In the latest case, police have refused to issue statements on the investigation, citing concerns that media reporting may be inspiring "copy-cat" actions in disturbed people.
"If journalists want to do their own investigation in the neighbourhood, that is their business. We are not going to help them," an officer told the ANP news agency.
The Council for Child Protection has set up special teams of social workers and psychologists to respond to calls and assess indications of looming family tragedies.
"If we can get signals of real problems we can send in the teams. It gives us added expertise and helps us assess and deal with any danger quickly," the spokeswoman said.

Danger signals looked for could include un-reconciled grief, violent outbursts in the home and problems dealing with divorce and custody issues, she said. Apart from calls to the Council, regular case workers would be expected to be extra vigilant.

The organisation was concerned about the influence of the media, but reluctant to jump to conclusions. "There is no scientific research we can look to here, so we just really don't know," the spokeswoman said.
